title: When every feature makes sense, but the product doesn’t

To submit your story: https://tinyurl.com/bootspub1 Product Design UX Product Management Collaboration Product Strategy When every feature makes sense, but the product doesn’t How teams settle disagreements, and who ends up paying for it. Navid Borjian 4 min read · Oct 26, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Image by author Picture a collaboration app that you open to find one shared document. The home screen leads with recent activity. A banner introduces a new assistant. A notification badge pulls you toward a conversation you weren’t looking for. Any one of these could be defended in a design review. Together, they stand between you and the document. Most product teams have seen a version of this, and nobody involved set out to make the product harder to use. In a recent interview with David Senra, Meta’s Alexandr Wang described keeping the team behind Muse , Meta’s new AI assistant, small and focused: fewer than 200 people across the model and the product. His argument was that users can tell when a product is a mixture of competing visions . Muse reached #1 on the US App Store within ten days of launch, though much more than focus went into that, including model quality, reliability work, timing, and Meta’s distribution. Press enter or click to view image in full size Credit: Meta What interests me is that Muse is itself a big-company product. Wang’s account suggests that a large company can preserve a focused product vision when it deliberately organizes around one point of view. That challenges the assumption that working at scale has to mean blending everyone’s preferences into the experience. How everyone’s idea gets in One team wants conversations to be more visible. Another wants people to discover new features. Someone in leadership feels the product should be more exciting. Each proposal has reasoning behind it, and they all want the same surface. The quickest way through that disagreement is often to give everyone something. A banner here, a tab there, another option in the menu. The meeting ends and the team moves on. The user wasn’t in that meeting. They have to work out what matters, where to start, and how the pieces relate. Reviewed one at a time, each addition holds up. The cost appears only when someone tries to finish a single task and has to hunt across the product to do it. In design reviews, I’ve noticed that the proposals that make it in aren’t always the best-supported ones. Some come from research or a real user problem. Others arrive as a sentence like “People won’t notice this unless we make it bigger” or “This screen feels too empty.” That second kind is rarely labeled as opinion. It tends to sound like a fact about users. Intuition isn’t the problem. Designers, product managers, and engineers all rely on it, because no team can research every decision. The trouble starts when confidence stands in for evidence. An idea can make it into the product because someone argued for it confidently, rather than because it fits the product well. A focused direction gives the team something to decide against. It lets someone say that a feature is useful but belongs elsewhere in the workflow, or in a different product. It also makes losing an argument easier to accept, because people can see the reason. Preferences and constraints The obvious objection is that a single direction can protect a single blind spot. Whoever holds the vision can be as attached to unexamined assumptions as anyone else. I think the answer depends on what kind of input is being weighed. Some input is preference: make it bigger, add more options, make it feel more exciting. A clear direction should filter that. Other input is constraint. When a privacy review finds a risk to people’s account data, or an accessibility review shows that an interaction shuts out screen reader users, that isn’t a competing vision. It’s a condition the vision has to meet, even if meeting it adds steps or delays a launch. The harder case is when the vision itself is wrong about what people want. There, the safeguard isn’t consensus but evidence. Wang describes user testing and evaluations of specific agent behaviors as part of how Muse was built. If testing shows the vision is wrong, the vision should change. That’s different from giving everyone a piece of the screen to keep the peace. Doing this is harder than it sounds, since the person holding the vision often decides what counts as evidence. Who settles the argument Products don’t usually get confusing because of one bad decision. More often, it’s a lot of good decisions that were never looked at together. A clear direction helps a team look at them together. Without one, the team settles its disagreement in a meeting, and the user has to deal with the result every time they open the app. Product Design UX Product Management Collaboration Product Strategy -- -- 1 Written by Navid Borjian 17 followers · 16 following Product designer simplifying complex systems.
